What it does

SlewRateLimiter(3) lets the value change 3 per second: 0 to full in 1/3 s.

Lower acceleration means less wheel slip and less tipping.

5

Control theory

The order of the stick steps matters

FeelRobotContainer.java

  private double shapedForward() {

    double x = -driver.getLeftY();

1   x = MathUtil.applyDeadband(x, DEADBAND);

2   x = MathUtil.copyDirectionPow(x, STICK_EXPONENT);

3   return forwardLimiter.calculate(x * DRIVE_SCALE);

  }

   

  private double shapedTurn() {

    double x = -driver.getRightX();

1   x = MathUtil.applyDeadband(x, DEADBAND);

2   x = MathUtil.copyDirectionPow(x, STICK_EXPONENT);

3   return x * TURN_SCALE;

  }

1

Deadband first

Throw away drift before anything else sees it.

2

Then the curve

copyDirectionPow keeps the sign, so reverse works.

3

Scale, then limit

Now 0.7 stays 0.7 at full stick, and the limiter sees the final value.

7

Control theory

Three gains predict the volts a drivetrain needs

Volts = kS + kV × speed + kA × acceleration. Deck 6 did this for an arm.

kS: friction

The volts needed to start moving. We assume 1 V.

kV: speed

Back-EMF grows with speed, so speed costs volts: 2.34 V per m/s.

kA: acceleration

The extra volts needed while gaining speed: 0.56 V per m/s².

10

Programming

One speed loop runs each side of the drivetrain

SpeedLoop.java

  /** Call once per loop. Returns the volts for this side. */

  public double calculate(double measured, double goal) {

    // The volts we can predict: kS, kV and kA.

1   double ffVolts =

1       feedforward.calculateWithVelocities(lastGoal, goal);

    // The volts we couldn't: P works on what is left over.

2   double pidVolts = pid.calculate(measured, goal);

3   lastGoal = goal;

4   return MathUtil.clamp(

4       ffVolts + pidVolts, -MAX_VOLTS, MAX_VOLTS);

  }

1

Feedforward

Two goals in a row give it the speed and the acceleration.

2

P

Works on what is left. KP is 6 volts per m/s of error.

3

Remember the goal

This is why each side gets its own object.

4

Add, then clamp

Volts add together, and a motor only gets 12.

Deck 9 · Advanced controls

11

Common mistake

One side of the drive runs away

What you see

You enable the speed loop, and one side slams to full speed. The robot spins or curves hard.

Why it happens

The sides are mirror images, so one encoder counts backward. Speeding up looks like slowing down, so P pushes harder.

The fix

Disabled, wheels up: turn each wheel forward by hand. Both speeds must rise. If one falls, flip it with setReverseDirection.

14

Programming

The arm loop can move onto the SPARK MAX

SparkArmSubsystem.java

  private static SparkMaxConfig sparkConfig() {

    SparkMaxConfig config = ArmConfig.base();

    config.closedLoop

1       .p(SPARK_KP).d(SPARK_KD)

        .outputRange(-MAX_OUTPUT, MAX_OUTPUT);

    config.closedLoop.feedForward

2       .kCos(KG) // an arm uses kCos, not REV's kG

3       .kCosRatio(1.0 / GEAR_RATIO); // NEO turns to arm turns

    return config;

  }

   

  private void setGoal(double goal) {

    goalRad = MathUtil.clamp(goal, SOFT_MIN_RAD, SOFT_MAX_RAD);

4   double rotations = armRadToMotorRotations(goalRad);

4   closedLoop.setSetpoint(rotations, ControlType.kPosition);

  }

1

Native units

p is duty cycle per NEO rotation. kP 30 is 0.26. Start low.

2

kCos, not kG

WPILib’s kG is REV’s kCos. REV’s kG is for elevators.

3

kCosRatio

NEO rotations to arm rotations: 1 / 60. The sensor must read 0 at flat.

4

Send it once

Goals are in NEO rotations. One message over CAN, then the SPARK does the work.

Deck 9 · Advanced controls

15

Best practice

Learn the loop in Java, then move it

Get a new loop right on the roboRIO, then move it to the controller.

Java loops are easy to log, change and try in the simulator. A controller loop is quicker and fresher, but its gains use other units, so you tune it again.

Deck 9 · Advanced controls

17

Where to go next

State-space and LQR are the next step up

State-space control describes a mechanism with a small math model, and kV and kA are already one. LQR then picks the feedback gains from how much error and how many volts you will accept.

The trade-off: you choose how much error and voltage to accept, not the gains.

Already in use: SysId uses LQR for the P and D gains it suggests.

WPILib’s advice: pick the easiest strategy that works on the field.
